articles.title: Republican lawmaker pushes Hegseth impeachment, Pentagon chief says 'not worried'
articles.summary: Republican Congressman Thomas Massie on Monday moved to force a vote in the US House of Representatives on impeaching defence secretary Pete Hegseth,
articles.body: Republican Congressman Thomas Massie on Monday moved to force a vote in the US House of Representatives on impeaching defence secretary Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on fellow Republicans to take a stand on the future of one of President Donald Trump's key Cabinet members.The move comes days after sweeping midterm election losses cost Republicans control of both chambers of Congress, raising the prospect of a broader Democratic push to hold Hegseth accountable for the administration's war in Iran.Hegseth, meanwhile, has dismissed the impeachment threat, saying he is "not worried" about the move and is prepared to defend the Trump administration's military actions in Iran.Speaking to reporters on Tuesday after delivering a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, Hegseth described the impeachment push as politically motivated and said his critics disagreed with the administration's record."There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he said.He added that he was willing to defend the administration's military decisions, saying, "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long.""We're not worried about that," Hegseth had said on Monday when asked about the impending resolution, adding that he would address the issue at a news conference on Tuesday.Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has been critical of President Donald Trump and the war in Iran, said Hegseth had violated the law by continuing military operations for more than 90 days without congressional approval."By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Massie said.The congressman first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September and is now pushing for a vote following last week's midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Republicans will retain control until January, when the new Congress takes office.Massie said his move was intended to press Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control and launch their own impeachment proceedings."My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials.""President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he added.The impeachment effort is expected to face an uphill battle, although Massie is likely to receive support from Democrats. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeaching Hegseth. However, Massie would still need support from members of his own party.Massie has also accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and disregarding congressional resolutions on war powers.The House has passed a War Powers resolution multiple times this year seeking to prevent Trump from taking further military action in Iran, with Massie supporting the measures.Under House rules, Speaker Mike Johnson must schedule consideration of Massie's resolution within two days of its introduction, which was expected later on Monday. The House can vote on the resolution, refer it to a committee or set it aside.Impeachment of a Cabinet secretary is rare. The House has voted to impeach only two Cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not agree to remove either of them. Removing Hegseth would require approval from both chambers.Meanwhile, Hegseth defended the administration's decision to launch military action against Iran, arguing that it was necessary to confront Tehran's nuclear ambitions."Someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon," he said, adding that "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."Asked about Vice President JD Vance attributing the Republicans' midterm losses partly to the Iran war, Hegseth pointed to Trump's statement that he would take the same action again, saying, "I agree."He also echoed a position expressed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio a day earlier, saying, "It doesn't have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary."You use AI every day. articles.title: Driver plows into North Carolina cycling group, killing 1 and injuring many others
articles.summary: A driver allegedly crossed the center line in Wake County, North Carolina, striking a group of cyclists and killing one before fleeing the scene. The man has been arrested.
articles.body: A driver plowed into a crowd of bicyclists in Wake County, North Carolina, early Sunday morning, killing one cyclist and injuring a number of others. The North Carolina State Highway Patrol (NCSHP) told Fox News Digital that troopers responded to the crash in Apex at about 9:39 a.m. Sunday. A black Infiniti driven by the suspect was traveling west along Optimist Farm Road when it "crossed the center line and struck a group of cyclists who were traveling east," an NCSHP official said. DEADLY CRASH KILLS TWO AS PLANE PLUNGES INTO ‘BALL OF FLAMES’ NEAR SUBURBAN GOLF COURSE "The passenger vehicle then continued traveling away from the scene before running off the left side of the roadway and colliding with a ditch approximately one-half mile away from the initial crash scene," the official added. The driver struck a number of cyclists in a group of about 30 riders, according to the Holly Springs Fire Department, as reported by several outlets. Some were treated at the scene, while others were taken to local hospitals. An NCSHP official told Fox News Digital that the cyclists "suffered injuries ranging from minor to serious, several of whom were transported to local hospitals for treatment." Approximately a dozen cyclists were injured in the incident, the same official said Monday. MOM OF 2 WHO DIED RESCUING SONS DURING BAHAMAS SNORKELING TRIP IS IDENTIFIED The driver, identified as Donald Robert Morris-Jones, 76, was charged with multiple offenses, including seven counts of felony serious injury by vehicle and eight counts of felony hit-and-run, officials said. He also faces charges of felony death by vehicle, driving while impaired, reckless driving and driving left of center. "Impairment is suspected to be a factor in the crash," an official told Fox News Digital. Morris-Jones was transported to the Wake County Detention Center, where he was being held on a $1 million secured bond. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The cyclist killed in the crash was identified as Patrick Allen Turner, 63, of Cary, North Carolina. The tragedy has also shaken North Carolina's cycling community. In a Facebook post, Cycle North Carolina, a statewide organization that hosts recreational cycling events, said Turner's death "makes this tragedy hit especially close to home." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Our hearts are with Patrick’s family and friends, as well as everyone else involved and impacted by this tragedy. We cannot begin to imagine the pain and shock they are experiencing," the organization wrote. "Please take care of one another [and] look out for your fellow cyclists." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Shaun King, board chair of Bike Durham, told ABC11 he first learned of the crash through concerned messages from friends and family. "We feel very vulnerable in this moment because this harm that our CCC community members are feeling right now could have happened to any of us," he told the outlet. articles.title: Pope draws 2.5 million to Mass in Argentina and tells people with disabilities they are a blessing
articles.summary: The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy.
articles.body: BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Pope Leo XIV visited a home for people with disabilities Monday and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden, as he pressed his call for Argentina to care for its most vulnerable in a symbolic rebuke of President Javier Milei’s austerity measures. Before drawing an estimated 2.5 million people to his first Mass in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre grounds. The center, known as the “city of charity,” has been hit hard by Milei’s austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina’s estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net. Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society. “You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life,” Leo said in the center’s chapel. “A nation’s progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” he added. Argentina’s Congress overrode Milei’s veto last year to pass a law increasing funding for disability care. But his administration has resisted implementation, citing concerns that it would undermine his hard-won fiscal balance. Care homes such as Cottolengo are still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars. Leo’s visit comes days before the Senate is due to consider legislation that would set aside money for disability benefits in next year’s budget. Milei opposes the measure. Given the circumstances, it was deeply significant that Leo chose to start his visit to Argentina by meeting with the Cottolengo guests, said Kuyen Rolon Rey, a volunteer at the home. “The people here deserve this grace,” Rolon Rey said. “Choosing such a small place, but big if measured with love, makes us very happy.” The pressure and media attention surrounding the papal visit paid off, at least partially, said Fernando Montero, who oversees the home’s disability services. Just over a week ago, the government paid Cottolengo Don Orione about 828 million pesos (roughly $535,000) for medications, diapers and food, covering about four months at the home, he said. The first papal Mass in nearly 40 years The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope, fulfilling the unfinished legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy. For many Argentines, though, the day’s highlight was Leo’s late-morning Mass at the Monumento a los Españoles, which the Vatican said drew 2.5 million people, Leo’s biggest liturgical turnout to date. The same site hosted the last papal Mass in Argentina, celebrated by St. John Paul II nearly 40 years ago. Thousands arrived at midnight to secure a good spot for Leo’s first Mass in Argentina. It got underway under blue skies on a day declared as a national holiday to allow people to attend and relieve normal commuting traffic around the central site. Among those in the VIP seats were Milei and his sister, Karina Milei, the secretary-general of the presidency. In his homily, Leo said Argentine families are facing situations of joblessness, violence and addictions, but are still the bedrock of society. “Do not give in to those who dismiss the Christian family as outdated. On the contrary, today more than ever, it remains a pillar amid the many insecurities of our time,” he said. Isabel Martín, 73, came with her parish group from San Andrés Avelino. She said she was praying for Leo to “touch the heart” of Milei, whose spending cuts have also hit pensioners hard. “The pope was very specific in his message yesterday,” she said, referring to Leo’s inaugural speech to Milei. “The weakest cannot be the ones carrying the burden of the adjustment, especially poor retirees. If anyone can make him reconsider, it’s the pope.” Argentina’s minimum pension is approximately $300, about a quarter of what an older adult needs to cover medicine, housing and food. Leo’s message was also resonating with younger Argentines, who have shown the sharpest decline in Catholic practice of any age group. Margarita Lanús celebrated her 16th birthday Monday while waiting for Leo’s Mass, sharing a cake on the sidewalk with her large family. “I really like that he says things as they are; he goes straight to the point,” she said. A message about an economy that serves Upon his arrival Sunday and with Milei at his side, Leo cited Francis’ frequent refrain that money must serve and not rule: “The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy,” Leo said in his first speech in Argentina. It’s a message Leo is expected to repeat later Monday when he meets with business leaders, union representatives and leaders of popular movements at the Catholic University of Argentina. Among those invited are domestic manufacturers battered by cheap imports since Milei scrapped long-standing trade barriers, and members of Argentina’s largest labor confederation, who took their worries over job losses and shrinking wages to the Vatican in September. Since Milei took office in late 2023, his austerity agenda has made him an icon of the global conservative backlash against the liberal establishment. Much like its counterparts in the Trump administration, Milei’s government has portrayed the cuts to disability programs as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy. Milei’s administration brushed off any suggestion of a rebuke in Leo’s comments. When asked whether the pope had criticized the government, Cabinet chief Diego Santilli said, “No, it’s everything we’ve been working on.” Opposition leaders heard a pope taking Milei to task, though some were careful not to turn it into a political fight. “I don’t want to frame it as discord or dispute,” said Buenos Aires province Gov. Axel Kicillof, the most powerful elected official in the left-leaning Peronist opposition, who welcomed the pope to the Cottolengo on Monday. “Let them listen to him, those who had their ears closed.”

articles.title: Spalding weathervane restored and back in place
articles.summary: The 19th Century weathervane has been placed back on Spalding Gentlemen's Society rooftop.
articles.body:
A "very visual symbol" of Spalding's history is back on a museum rooftop after 150 hours of restoration.

Dating back to 1810, the weathervane, mostly made of copper, depicts a three-masted seagoing vessel.

It was placed back onto Spalding Gentlemen's Society museum roof on Broad Street on 4 November after it was refurbished by one of the museum's members, Robert Frost.

Dustin Frazier Wood, head of collections and operations at the society said: "That ship really represented a very long, hundreds of years history of shipping in Spalding and its connections with the world."

The weathervane was originally situated in the former Ship Warehouse in Double Street before it was demolished in 1964. It was first displayed on the museum's rooftop in 1996.

Wood said the restoration was needed as the weathervane had been "exposed to the elements for nearly 200 years".

He said: "This is a place in theory you could board ship and go out to sea around the world as so many people in Spalding did.

"For the town it's that very visible symbol of the history of the place and its connection to the wider world."

Spalding Gentlemen's Society began in 1710 with informal meetings at a coffee house in Abbey Yard, after it was founded by Maurice Johnson of Ayscoughfee Hall.

The museum and building is currently undergoing a renovation which was launched in 2025 and the first phase of the project is funded by a Museum Estate & Development Fund (MEND) grant, the society said.

It comes after the society said the building was "subsiding and placing strain on the original structure" following extensions.

"These essential works will help secure the building's future for generations to come and enable the society's museum to be repaired, refurbished, and fully re-displayed for the first time in over a century," the society said.

The society added that the re-erection of the weathervane "marked a step towards the museum reopening for visitors in spring 2027".

Collections in the museum represent all time periods and all seven continents, Wood said.

articles.summary: The case comes as the Ivy League institution grapples with a high-profile scandal over a different civil case filed in September by a woman identified in court papers as Jane Doe.
articles.body: An ongoing lawsuit filed in 2023 alleges that Cornell University permitted a male student to sexually abuse two women and potentially others. The lawsuit, filed by two alleged victims against Cornell and the alleged offender, said the university failed to protect the accusers and others from persistent sexual assault, sexual abuse and other misconduct. “Throughout his enrollment in the school and on campus, the [defendant] sexually abused, sexually assaulted, and perpetrated egregious sexual misconduct against college students, specifically on the Plaintiffs,” according to a lawsuit filed in Tompkins County Supreme Court on Nov. 10, 2023. The lawsuit was first reported by New York Focus. A judge on the case previously denied motions to dismiss the lawsuit. Pretrial discovery proceedings are underway. “Cornell disputes any assertion that it failed to investigate reported sexual misconduct and absolutely rejects any assertion that it would have failed to act in response to multiple reports of such misconduct. The university has no further comment on this pending litigation,” according to a statement from a spokesperson for the school. The student’s attorney, Keith White, said his client’s responses to the allegations “are asserted in the responses filed in the lawsuit” and declined to comment further. The official response contains denials but no additional information. The plaintiffs in the case did not respond to requests for comment. One of the accusers said in an affidavit that she was sexually assaulted and abused by the alleged male student in September and October 2018 and that she filed a Title IX civil rights case against him around that time. The male student, whose name NBC News is withholding because he has not been charged criminally in this case, denied all allegations in court papers. The Title IX office received “numerous” other complaints against the same individual, according to a sworn statement from one of the women dated April 19, 2024. The other accuser said the male student “sexually, physically, and verbally assaulted me in his on-campus dorm room” on May 7, 2021. That alleged victim filed a Title IX complaint in August of that year but “no action was taken,” and the alleged offender continued to attend Cornell, the plaintiff wrote in a separate April 2024 submission. However, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, he was suspended by the university and later transferred to a different school. It was not clear what led to his suspension. Title IX is a federal law that prohibits gender-based discrimination. It is commonly used as a way for colleges and universities to adjudicate allegations of sexual assault outside of the criminal justice system. A person who is accused can face both civil proceedings under Title IX and criminal proceedings in local courts. The pending case comes to light as the Ivy League institution grapples with a high-profile scandal over a different civil case filed in September by a woman identified in court papers as Jane Doe. Jane Doe alleged that she was gang-raped and forced to do drugs at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. An internal investigation for that case resulted in two expulsions and other repercussions, but no criminal charges were filed. New York Attorney General Letitia James was tapped by the governor on Oct. 1 to lead a new criminal investigation. Last week, James announced that a former federal prosecutor was recruited by her office to lead the inquiry. The 2023 case came to light days after the faculty senate issued a vote of no confidence in the ability of Cornell administrators to handle what the sponsors called an “ongoing crisis of sexual assault.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

articles.title: Tyler Robinson: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk shooter set for June 2028
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.
articles.body:
The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.

Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.

Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.

Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".

Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."

During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.

Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

articles.title: Judge issues order protecting Daughters of American Revolution chapter that only allows biological women
articles.summary: The Daughters of the American Revolution face a temporary restraining order blocking them from disbanding a chapter over blocking transgender membership.
articles.body: A judge has issued a temporary restraining order stopping the leadership of The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) from disbanding a local Texas chapter that only allows biological women to join, according to a legal advocacy organization. The Martha Laird chapter had fought to bar transgender women – biological men who identify as women – from joining its ranks. The national leadership of DAR voted in early October to disband this chapter, citing violations of its national bylaws. The Heritage Foundation's Legal Action Center, which represented the Texas chapter in suing the national organization, celebrated the court's decision. "The court's order is an important victory for the Martha Laird Chapter and the women who stood up for the principle that a women’s organization should be for women," Lea Patterson, senior litigation counsel with Heritage, wrote. "National DAR leadership tried to silence these women by disbanding their 84-year-old chapter. We are grateful the court has stepped in to protect the chapter while this fight continues." KAPPA KAPPA GAMMA MEMBER SAYS TRANSGENDER MEMBERSHIP POLICY UNDERMINES SORORITY SISTERHOOD She continued, "DAR headquarters tried to punish its members for speaking out, shut down legitimate debate, and strip a chapter of its assets without a fair process. These women followed DAR’s own procedures to advocate for change. They deserve to be heard, not punished for standing up for their convictions." The National Society Daughters of the American Revolution confirmed to Fox News Digital that the organization had voted to disband the local Texas chapter but denied it was due to its views on membership and said it was acting in compliance with its national bylaws. "The National Society Daughters of the American Revolution (NSDAR) stands by the October 10, 2026, decision of its National Board of Management, which was made under the authority established in the National Bylaws," the organization told Fox News Digital. "The decision was based on the Martha Laird Chapter’s use of the DAR name and its official chapter leadership, communications, and governance processes to promote the objectives of a separate advocacy organization. It was not based on the personal views or advocacy of individual members." "The court’s temporary restraining order does not determine the validity of the National Board’s decision. NSDAR is complying with the order and remains confident that the National Board acted within its authority under the National Bylaws and that its decision will withstand judicial review," the statement read. The group did not respond to an additional request for comment about the separate advocacy organization claim. LEADER OF FIRM THAT WON SCOTUS WOMEN'S SPORTS CASES OPENS UP ON DEALING WITH LIBERAL MEDIA, TITLE IX LAWSUITS Political strategist and former senior Senate advisor Mary Marslender said the judge's ruling was proper. "It shouldn’t take a court order to state the obvious: the Daughters of the American Revolution should be for women, not men. Changing a label doesn’t change biological reality. My daughters shouldn’t have to grow up in a world where their sex is treated as a choice and their spaces as negotiable," she told Fox News Digital. "Organizations created by and for women should not be pressured to ignore basic facts. The Texas chapter defended common sense, and I applaud the judge’s decision to halt this misguided effort to undermine a historic women’s group." articles.title: 81-year-old sci-fi author M. John Harrison wins the 2026 Booker Prize
articles.summary: The British author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize, considered one of the most prestigious literary awards for a work of fiction.
articles.body: The British author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize, considered one of the most prestigious literary awards for a work of fiction. At 81 years old, he is also the oldest author ever to be awarded with the honor. The announcement was made during a ceremony at London’s Old Billingsgate, the site of a former fish market, on Monday. Harrison will receive a prize of £50,000 ($67,000). This year’s judging panel, chaired by historian Mary Beard, featured writers Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood, critic Rebecca Liu and musician Jarvis Cocker, front man of the British band Pulp. Harrison’s post-apocalyptic turn, titled “The End of Everything,” takes place in the English coastal town of Dalston-on-Sea in the not-too-distant future, during the occupation of mysterious lifeforms called the iGhetti. Though much about the visitors’ origins remains ambiguous, the author told BBC radio that the real-world event that sparked the plot was the 2008 financial crisis. At 198 pages, it was the slimmest of the six shortlisted books. “‘The End of Everything’” can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism; whatever the reader is looking for can be found here, albeit told at a slant and with a twist,” the jury wrote in a Q&A published ahead of the announcement. Harrison’s win could be considered the first time a science fiction novel has been awarded the prize. Though the 2024 winner “Orbital” takes place aboard a space station, the philosophical novel is murkier in its categorization. Regardless, this year marks a rare recognition of the genre and honors an author who has published within it for more than five decades. Harrison began his “Virconium” series in 1971, set on a futuristic Earth, and continued writing about the fictional city in novels and stories through 1984. Among his other works, he completed the “Kefahuchi Tract” trilogy between 2002 and 2012. This year was the first time he was nominated for the Booker Prize. “You talk glibly about your life being changed, but it’s weird when it happens. I feel like a proper writer at last, totally lacking in confidence,” Harrison said as he accepted the award. Harrison beat five other finalists, including the betting market’s favorites Marlon James and Douglas Stuart, both former winners. Harrison was selected from 163 submissions that were narrowed down to a 13-book longlist and six finalists, announced in September. The shortlist included James “The Disappearers” and Stuart’s “John of John” as well as Luke Kennard’s “Black Bag,” Elizabeth Strout’s “The Things We Never Say,” and Rebecca Perry’s “May We Feed the King.” Ahead of Monday’s ceremony, the Booker Prize Foundation’s chief executive, Gaby Wood, said that the shortlisted books were unified by a question: “What can we know of each other, what do we infer or assume, what are we prepared to see?” “Despite the great range in their styles and subjects, in all of these novels we find forms of isolation: relationships breaking down or withheld, people harboring secrets or pain, characters closing themselves off from others or attempting to reach beyond their solitude towards them,” Wood said, according to a statement on the Prize’s official website. First awarded in 1969, the Booker Prize was originally only open to writers from the UK, Ireland or Commonwealth nations. From the 2014 prize onwards, eligibility was opened to include English-language authors of any nationality, as long as the nominated work is published in the UK or Irish markets. Its sister award, the International Booker Prize, is meanwhile awarded for a work of fiction that has been translated into English. Last year’s Booker Prize went to author David Szalay’s “Flesh,” a sparsely written novel recounting a taciturn Hungarian immigrant’s journey from poverty to the upper echelons of London high society. Other notable winners include Salman Rushdie, William Golding, Ian McEwan, Arundhati Roy and Kazuo Ishiguro. Margaret Atwood previously held the distinction of the oldest author to be honored, when she was jointly recognized at age 79 for “The Testaments.” She shared the 2019 Booker Prize with Bernardine Evaristo, author of “Girl, Woman, Other.” This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Trump signals no Iran strikes coming after meeting Qatari leader
articles.summary: President Trump downplayed the possibility of renewed military action against Iran but said the U.S. was maintaining its wartime posture in the Middle East to protect allied Arab and Gulf partners, speaking from the White House on Monday. Trump’s comments came following a meeting with the primary interlocutor with Iran, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed…
articles.body:
President Trump downplayed the possibility of renewed military action against Iran but said the U.S. was maintaining its wartime posture in the Middle East to protect allied Arab and Gulf partners, speaking from the White House on Monday.

Trump’s comments came following a meeting with the primary interlocutor with Iran, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

Trump said America’s allies prefer the U.S. to maintain the naval blockade and a land blockade that amounts to a “status quo,” in a post on his social media site Truth Social, and later in remarks at the White House.

“We have the greatest military blockade ever. We have the new Iron Gate,” Trump said.

“Iron Gate is land, so by land and by sea, and we will take care of business.”

The U.S. in recent weeks has been carrying out limited strikes on Iran, on the southern island of Queshm, which the Trump administration describes as defensive.

Trump said the U.S. would remain in the Middle East to help defend Arab and Gulf partners from Iranian attacks.

“We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they are not hurt,” he told reporters in the White House briefing room.

“It’s ending quicky, but we want to take care of people that have been very good to us over the years.”

Trump said the Iranians were reaching out on negotiations. On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iranian demands to end the war were unacceptable, “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

Iranian officials have called for the U.S. to lift its blockade and lift sanctions to restart negotiations.

articles.title: Man killed in fiery Kentucky jet crash told daughter of trouble in midair
articles.summary: Before he died, a Wisconsin father radioed his daughter about issues he was having after takeoff on Sunday, Nov. 8. Then his jet hit a ditch and caught fire in Kentucky.
articles.body: A 70-year-old Wisconsin man was killed in a fiery crash Sunday, Nov. 8, when his military-style jet plunged into a field in Mayfield, Kentucky, shortly after takeoff. The accident turned a cross-country flight alongside his daughter into a sudden tragedy. The pilot, identified as James Alan Michaels of Dousman, Wisconsin, and his 35-year-old daughter, Tonie Michaels, were flying separate L-39 Albatros jets. "The father and daughter were flying back to Wisconsin from Mississippi," the Graves County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS The pair had been at an air show and stopped at an airport in Mayfield to get fuel, the sheriff's office said. After takeoff, "they were gaining altitude and the deceased ... said he was having issues," the sheriff's office said. "He was going to turn and go back to the airport." Soon after, "he radioed ... that he was not going to be able to land," the sheriff's office said. "We think he tried to land in an open field," the sheriff's office said. However, at around 2:08 p.m., the plane went down just off Spence Chapel Road near Interstate 69 and Ky. 131. "It hit a ditch in that field," the sheriff's office said. "The ditch seems to be the cause of the main impact," the sheriff's office said. "The plane caught fire and actually rolled." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The pilot was the only person on the plane. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The daughter soon arrived at the scene, the sheriff's office said. "She turned around and landed back at the airport. [Then] she started making phone calls." The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital that Sunday's crash occurred around 2:25 p.m. local time, though local authorities recorded the crash time slightly earlier, at 2:08 p.m. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said its investigators will lead the probe into the crash. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER An investigator was expected to arrive at the scene Monday evening to document the site and examine the aircraft before it's recovered to a secure facility for further evaluation, the NTSB said. The NTSB said its investigations involve three primary areas: the pilot, the aircraft, and the operating environment. As part of the process, investigators will gather flight track data, air traffic control communications, aircraft maintenance records, witness statements and weather conditions, the agency said. It said investigators will also review the pilot’s license, ratings, recency of flight experience and 72-hour background check to determine if any issues could have affected his ability to safely operate the flight. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ During the on-scene phase of the investigative process, the NTSB does not determine or speculate about the cause of the accident, the agency said. A probable cause of the crash along with any contributing factors will be detailed in the final report, which is expected in 12 to 24 months, the NTSB said. Sixteen years prior to this accident, the same father and daughter duo survived a small-plane crash in a remote area of Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, WBAY News Report said at the time. On July 8, 2010, James Michaels was piloting a single-engine aircraft with his daughter as his passenger when they encountered a severe downdraft. The pair crash-landed in heavy timber in Forest Canyon while flying toward Aspen, the National Park Service Summary Report via NTSB Docket previously said. They used branches and the plane's sheared-off wreckage to build a shelter as they were stranded overnight during evening storms, The Denver Post reported at the time.

articles.title: Até quando vai o frio fora de época no Centro-Sul? | G1
articles.standfirst: Massa de ar polar derrubou as temperaturas no Sul, Sudeste e parte do Centro-Oeste. Frio deve perder força ao longo da semana, mas ainda há possibilidade de geada nas serras gaúcha e catarinense.
articles.summary: Massa de ar polar derrubou as temperaturas no Sul, Sudeste e parte do Centro-Oeste. Frio deve perder força ao longo da semana, mas ainda há possibilidade de geada nas serras do RS.
articles.body:
Pedestres tentam se proteger do frio no centro, da cidade de São Paulo, SP. — Foto: ALEXANDRE MARETTI/FUTURA PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

O frio fora de época que atingiu parte do Brasil nesta segunda-feira (9) deve começar a perder força nos próximos dias.

A previsão indica que as temperaturas devem subir gradualmente a partir desta terça-feira (10), principalmente no Sul, no Sudeste e em áreas do Centro-Oeste.

A mudança ocorre depois da passagem de uma frente fria intensa , que levou uma massa de ar polar para o interior do país e provocou temperaturas baixas para novembro, mês em que a primavera normalmente já é marcada por tardes mais quentes.

No Sul, os termômetros chegaram a apenas 0,9°C em Bom Jardim da Serra (SC) nesta última segunda-feira. Em São Francisco de Paula (RS), a mínima foi de 3,5°C. Também houve registro de geada na Serra Catarinense.

Segundo o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia ( Inmet ), o ar frio deve continuar influenciando o Sul e o Sudeste até pelo menos quarta-feira (11), mas sua intensidade tende a diminuir gradualmente.

Isso acontece porque o sistema de alta pressão associado à massa de ar polar deve se afastar em direção ao oceano Atlântico, permitindo a entrada de ventos mais quentes vindos do norte do continente.

A Climatempo também prevê uma recuperação das temperaturas ao longo da semana, principalmente a partir de quarta-feira no Sul. No Centro-Sul como um todo, o aquecimento deve ficar mais perceptível a partir de quinta-feira (12).

Mesmo assim, algumas regiões ainda devem registrar manhãs frias antes da volta do calor.

Nesta terça-feira (10), as temperaturas ainda devem permanecer baixas, principalmente no Sul e em áreas do Sudeste.

Em Curitiba (PR), a mínima prevista é de 9°C, enquanto a máxima deve chegar a 18°C. Na Serra Gaúcha e na Serra Catarinense, ainda existe possibilidade de geada isolada durante a madrugada e o início da manhã.

Em Porto Alegre (RS), a temperatura deve começar o dia em torno de 12°C a 15°C, mas pode alcançar 27°C durante a tarde, indicando uma recuperação mais rápida do calor.

No Sudeste, São Paulo (SP) deve registrar temperaturas entre 12°C e 22°C nesta terça-feira. No Rio de Janeiro (RJ), a máxima deve ficar próxima de 23°C, enquanto Belo Horizonte (MG) ainda pode ter um dia mais frio, com mínima de 14°C e máxima de 18°C, segundo a Climatempo.

Em parte do Centro-Oeste, o ar frio também começa a perder intensidade. Campo Grande (MS), por exemplo, pode amanhecer com 17°C, mas a máxima deve alcançar 31°C durante a tarde.

Já na quarta-feira (11), a tendência é de temperaturas mais elevadas em boa parte do Centro-Sul.

Em São Paulo, a máxima deve chegar aos 25°C, enquanto o Rio de Janeiro pode registrar 27°C. Curitiba ainda deve ter uma manhã fria, mas os termômetros podem alcançar 21°C durante a tarde.

Porto Alegre deve registrar máxima de 28°C, e Florianópolis (SC) pode chegar aos 25°C.

Mapa mostra previsão de chuva para esta terça (10/11) em todo o Brasil. — Foto: CPTEC/Reprodução

No Sul, a previsão é de tempo mais firme durante o começo da semana. A partir de quarta-feira, novas áreas de instabilidade podem se formar, inicialmente de maneira isolada. No Rio Grande do Sul, há possibilidade de temporais localizados e eventual queda de granizo.

No Sudeste, a chuva ainda deve atingir principalmente Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro e Espírito Santo nesta terça-feira.

Na quarta, as precipitações tendem a diminuir, embora a nebulosidade continue elevada em algumas áreas.

Já no Centro-Oeste, o calor e a umidade devem favorecer pancadas de chuva em Goiás, Mato Grosso e no Distrito Federal. Mato Grosso do Sul, por outro lado, deve ter períodos maiores de tempo firme antes do retorno das instabilidades.

A frente fria que provocou o frio no Centro-Sul também continua influenciando o tempo na Bahia, onde a previsão indica chuva forte e persistente, principalmente no litoral sul.

Entre Ilhéus e Porto Seguro, os volumes acumulados podem superar 250 milímetros até quinta-feira (12), segundo a Climatempo.

No Norte, o calor deve continuar predominando ao longo da semana, apesar da previsão de pancadas de chuva em vários estados. Na terça-feira (10), Amazonas, Rondônia, Tocantins e áreas do Pará podem registrar temporais.

Em Boa Vista (RR), a temperatura pode chegar aos 38°C na terça-feira. Na quarta (11), a chuva deve atingir outras áreas da região, mas o calor e a sensação de abafamento continuam.

No Nordeste, o calor também deve predominar, principalmente no interior. Na terça-feira, há previsão de pancadas de chuva no centro e sul do Maranhão e em áreas do Piauí, acompanhadas de trovoadas em alguns pontos.

Na quarta-feira, o tempo deve continuar firme em grande parte da região, com temperaturas elevadas. Em Teresina (PI), a máxima pode chegar aos 39°C, enquanto Fortaleza (CE) e João Pessoa (PB) podem registrar 34°C.

articles.title: 5 takeaways from Trump’s surprise White House briefing
articles.summary: President Trump carried out a surprise press briefing at the White House on Monday, teasing reporters with an appearance by UFC head Dana White — to whom he offered the job as press secretary — and providing a combative response to the GOP’s stunning defeat in the midterm elections. The president took a wide range…
articles.body:
President Trump carried out a surprise press briefing at the White House on Monday, teasing reporters with an appearance by UFC head Dana White — to whom he offered the job as press secretary — and providing a combative response to the GOP’s stunning defeat in the midterm elections.

The president took a wide range of questions on foreign policy, including Iran, Russia and Cuba. He addressed allegations of Chinese spying on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and lashed out at critics of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is facing an impeachment vote in the House.

Here are five takeaways from the president’s impromptu press conference:

Trump downplayed renewing major military operations against Iran but signaled no end to the more than eight-month war. The president said he was maintaining a naval blockade against Iran, escalating a land blockade — dubbing it “Operation Iron Gate” — and offering protection to U.S. allies in the region.

Trump said the war was “ending quickly,” but added, “we want to take care of people that have been very good to us over the years.”

The president’s remarks followed a White House meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has served as a primary go-between for Washington and Iran.

Trump said he was maintaining the “status quo” in the region by keeping U.S. troops present but said Iranian officials are talking to the U.S. “and they’re talking very politely, and we’ll see what happens.”

Trump added that forces are “locked and loaded, and hopefully we don’t have to use them.”

Trump offered a vocal defense of Hegseth, lambasting Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who reintroduced eight articles of impeachment earlier Monday, as a “stone-cold loser.”

“He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate or anything that he’s doing. The guy’s a stone-cold loser,” the president told reporters during the press conference.

Trump claimed Hegseth “won” two wars, referring to the U.S. military operation to snatch Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and the conflict against Iran.

The president also said he would stand by Hegseth even if the Pentagon chief is impeached by the House of Representatives, an effort that will have massive Democratic Party backing.

“Yeah, I’ll stand by,” the president said in a response to a question from a reporter.

“He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won,” Trump added.

In his defense of Hegseth, the president also questioned why Lloyd Austin, who served as the secretary of Defense during the Biden administration, was not impeached.

“What about good old Lloyd? Why didn’t we go after him? Why didn’t we go after the people that disappeared? They’re in charge of the military, and they disappeared,” Trump said. “Nobody knew … had any idea that nothing happened to him.”

Austin faced heat in early 2024 after revelation that he had prostate cancer surgery and was later hospitalized in intensive care due to complications, whereabouts that then-President Biden, Cabinet members and his deputy knew about.

White seemed more than happy to join Trump in the press briefing room. When he got behind the podium, he told reporters that he’s “always wanted to do this.”

“Who has the first question?” the UFC head asked. “I have zero political aspirations.”

He said he was at a fight in London when Trump called him and told him he put the Truth Social post out, suggesting White could become the next press secretary.

“And the last 24 hours of my life has been insane,” White said. “Literally everybody, every media outlet was calling me, and I didn’t want to be disrespectful and say anything until he said something first.”

He said he didn’t tell the president “no” about taking the job.

“I don’t tell the president no to anything,” he said.

Trump said the joke Truth Social post came after a “very bad press day.”

“I don’t know why I thought of his name. He’s been my friend for a long time. I said, ‘You know, I think I’m going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,’” the president said. “And I sent it to a group of the press, and that was it. I was really kidding. And then they wrote the stories as though I wasn’t kidding.”

White was asked if he had any advice for Trump about the president’s proposed pardon for deceased Major League Baseball player Pete Rose. Rose served a short stint in prison for tax evasion. He was also banned from baseball in 1989 for betting on the sport.

Trump said “it’s fair” to pardon Rose because he was “very mistreated.”

At the end of the briefing, he once again asked if White wanted the position.

“Let me ask you the big question. Dana, would you like to be press secretary of the United States of America?” he said. “Look at the sign. You’d have this behind you all the time. The White House, Washington. Would you like that, or do you just want to stay with this ridiculous UFC?”

White thanked Trump for the offer but reiterated that he doesn’t want to be in politics.

“I am devastated to hear this,” Trump said. “Goodbye, everybody.”

Trump said he talked to Huang on Monday, following the Nvidia CEO announcing he’d had an affair with a woman that the intelligence community reportedly alleges was a Chinese spy.

Trump called Huang “an honorable man” who “built a great American company.”

“I feel very confident he’ll be in good shape,” the president added.

Trump said he had no plans to bring up alleged Chinese corporate espionage in an expected summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.

Trump said he heard about Huang’s association with the alleged spy “not too long ago.”

“When I heard about — first of all, I was amazed, because I view him as a very high-quality person,” the president said.

Trump added that he wasn’t aware of the allegations when he traveled to China to meet Xi in May. Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in September.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a classified memo warning top Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to Beijing that Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported on Sunday.

Trump didn’t directly address a question on if he saw the memo, but added, “Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

Trump was adamantly against approving new wind turbines despite supporting the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act that aims to ease the passage of all forms of energy, including wind.

The bill faced a key procedural vote in the Senate on Monday.

“The permitting bill is a great bill that’s supposed to be bipartisan,” he said. “We are behind it 100 percent.”

But when he was specifically asked if he would support future wind turbines, he said, “No, I will not approve wind turbines.”

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” he told reporters. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

The bill is supported by Democrats in part because it includes support for renewable energy, like wind turbines. It aims to stop future administrations from revoking existing permits and discriminating against certain types of energy, like wind turbines.

When asked about Trump’s comments, a White House official said that the president stands behind the bill and that the administration has been working “in good faith with Senate Democrats for months.”

images.caption: President Trump gestures to Dana White, UFC’s president and CEO, as he speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
articles.summary: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
articles.body:
A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.

At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.

"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.

"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women .

Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.

Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.

We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.

The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.

He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.

Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves.

"Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men."

Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko .

Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2.

If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube

An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.

"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.

We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.

Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."

In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.

The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.

Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.

We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.

"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."

Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.

"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.

She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.

Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.

After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.

And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.

The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."

They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.

We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".

Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.

"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."

images.caption: Roza has decided to share her story with the BBC

articles.title: Verdict delayed in Honduras sex-trafficking case linked to disappearance
articles.summary: Angie Pena’s disappearance in 2022 exposed what prosecutors called a sex-trafficking network and state corruption.
articles.body:
A court in Honduras has delayed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Pena, a case that has raised concerns about impunity in transnational crimes.

On Monday, Honduras’s judiciary cited the need to review evidence and wait for the return of a court interpreter, who was out of the country. The decision has been delayed until November 20.

The verdict was expected that same day. Critics framed the unexpected delay as yet another hurdle in a case that has drawn comparisons to the crimes of the late Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender in the US accused of running a sex-trafficking ring.

Four men, including two US citizens, are on trial for crimes related to Pena’s disappearance four years ago.

Harold Green and William James Murdock, both from the US, face human-trafficking charges. Another US citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran citizen Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.

Honduran authorities have also sought an Interpol notice for another suspect, US citizen Antony Frank Grayson.

The Honduran public prosecutor’s office said the suspects are part of a network involved in crimes including drug trafficking and sex trafficking involving minors.

It alleges police and at least one judge helped facilitate the criminal network, without naming the officials.

Defence lawyers, however, have denied the men’s involvement and requested an acquittal.

Pena went missing on January 1, 2022, after setting out on a jet ski from West Bay on the Honduran island of Roatan, while vacationing with her family.

Authorities initially focused on a rescue mission at sea, treating her disappearance as a possible accident.

But the case expanded into a trafficking investigation after Pena’s jet ski was found in Belize, some 170km (90 nautical miles) away.

In August 2022, authorities investigating the disappearance found a minor in the Roatan house occupied by Johnston, who was later sentenced to 32 years for commercial sex trafficking and child pornography in a separate case.

An analysis by Honduran media found that the country was mentioned more than 100 times in the Epstein files, including multiple references to Roatan, from where Pena disappeared.

“There are many more women and girls who have been victims of trafficking networks, and those cases are silenced, they go unpunished,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights, which represents Pena’s family.

Lawyers representing the family have questioned the lack of transparency in the investigation and in the trial, which was not open to the press or the general public.

Postponing the verdict “fuels the perception of impunity, increases public distrust in state security institutions, and prolongs the suffering and vulnerability of affected families”, said former Honduran Vice Minister of Security Julissa Villanueva in a post on X.

Dereck McNeil, a key protected witness, was killed in August, spurring further concerns about the case.

In videos made public after his death, McNeil alleged corruption within a special unit of the public prosecutor’s office known as the ATIC.

He accused the unit of leaking information about the case and being linked to drug-trafficking networks.

The ATIC director has denied any corruption and said that the unit has not been involved in investigating Pena’s disappearance.

Villanueva, the former vice minister, told The Associated Press that she believes prosecutors mishandled the case from the start, pushing a “tunnel vision” explanation of what happened.

“There are connections with other larger networks, and only by making them public will this family be able to get justice,” said Villanueva.

“It’s not just Angie. It’s all those women around Angie. There are many.”

images.caption: A beach on the Honduran island of Roatan, from where Angie Pena went missing on a jet ski in 2022 [File: AP Photo]

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most shifting to India
articles.summary: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.
articles.body:
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.

In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.

Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.

The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.

On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".

Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".

The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".

Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.

Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.

The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

images.caption: Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson apologised for the "hard news" of 850 job cuts

articles.title: 'Cruise for life' ship Villa Vie Odyssey seized in Singapore
articles.summary: It comes weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end, leaving 200 guests stranded in Cambodia.
articles.body:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.

The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".

The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.

"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".

Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.

The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.

Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.

"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.

However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.

It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.

Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.

It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs

articles.title: ‘He won two wars’: Donald Trump rallies behind Hegseth amid impeachment push
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has thrown his support behind defence secretary Pete Hegseth as Republican Representative Thomas Massie pushes for a House vote
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has thrown his support behind defence secretary Pete Hegseth as Republican Representative Thomas Massie pushes for a House vote to impeach the Pentagon chief over his handling of the Iran war and other military operations.Trump attacked Massie during an unexpected appearance in the White House briefing room on Monday, hours after the Kentucky Republican filed eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth and read them aloud on the House floor.“Massie is a loser,” Trump said. “He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate or anything that he’s doing.”Also Read| Judge orders probe after 400 trees cut at Trump's Washington golf courseThe president also described Massie as a “stone cold loser” and said he would stand by Hegseth even if the House voted to impeach him.“Yeah, I’ll stand by,” Trump said. “He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.”Trump defended Hegseth's record, claiming that he had overseen successful military operations in Venezuela and Iran. The US operation in Venezuela led to the capture of former leader Nicolas Maduro in January, while the conflict with Iran is still ongoing.“Really, what has Hegseth done?” Trump said. “He won the war. He was in charge. He won the war in Venezuela, as I said, 48 minutes. It was flawless — nobody killed. And he certainly, I think, won the war in Iran.”Also Read| ‘Zero political aspirations’: UFC chief Dana White responds to Trump’s White House job offerLater, in a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, "Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth. With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!"The president's remarks came as Hegseth faces growing criticism over his role in the administration's military operations, including the war against Iran and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling vessels in the Caribbean.Why is Thomas Massie seeking Hegseth's impeachment?Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abusing his powers and carrying out unlawful military actions. The charges largely concern the Iran war but also refer to US operations in Yemen and Venezuela.Reading the resolution on the House floor, Massie accused Hegseth of having “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” and said he “remains a threat to the Constitution”.The articles also accuse the defence secretary of illegally launching the war against Iran and being responsible for civilian deaths in boat strikes targeting alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean, Politico reported.Hegseth has rejected the allegations. Last week, he described the impeachment effort as a sham by “a disgruntled defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies”.Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year, has been among the party members openly questioning Hegseth's handling of the conflict.Trump also took aim at Massie's electoral defeat, saying he had backed a challenger who had never run for office before and beaten the incumbent easily. He accused the lawmaker of having “a lot of hatred in his heart”.During the exchange, Trump also criticised CNN journalist Kaitlan Collins when she pressed him on Massie's allegations against Hegseth.“Massie’s a loser, just like you’re a loser at CNN, just like your ratings are a loser, Massie is a loser, stone cold loser,” he said.Also Read| ‘Locked and loaded’: Trump warns Iran as Tehran demands US ‘surrender’House vote expected as political battle intensifiesA vote on the impeachment resolution could take place by mid-week, although its prospects remain uncertain.House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has backed the measure, while Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has also endorsed the impeachment push.“Hegseth must stand trial before the Senate,” Schumer said.If most Democrats support the resolution, Massie would need the backing of only a small number of Republicans to secure impeachment in the House.However, Republican leaders have expressed reservations about holding the vote while military operations abroad are continuing. House Speaker Mike Johnson said impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that”.Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he was unsure why the vote was being held at this stage, adding that the Senate would deal with the matter depending on the House's decision.If the House impeaches Hegseth, the Senate would have to decide whether to dismiss the charges or hold a trial. Republicans retain control of both chambers until the new Congress convenes in January, when Democrats are set to take control.This is the second attempt by Massie in two months to remove Hegseth. articles.title: Cameroon sets date for twice-delayed legislative and local elections
articles.summary: President Paul Biya, the world’s oldest leader, sets February 7 for Cameroon’s delayed legislative and local polls.
articles.body:
Cameroon’s President Paul Biya has announced that legislative and local elections will be held in the country on February 7 next year.

Biya, who is 93, made the announcement in a decree read on public radio on Monday.

The decree comes at a tense moment for Cameroon, with authorities cracking down on the opposition, roughly a year after an election that handed Biya another term.

Biya, who has ruled Cameroon since 1982, is the world’s oldest head of state.

His re-election in October last year set off widespread protests that the authorities met with a violent crackdown.

Lawyers cited by Human Rights Watch said security forces detained up to 2,000 people, and some of those detained remain in custody, according to the AFP news agency.

Biya’s government has already postponed Cameroon’s legislative and local elections twice, forcing the extension of lawmakers’ terms to December 20 and those of municipal councillors to February 28, 2027.

The country is also awaiting a government reshuffle announced nearly a year ago and the appointment of a vice president. A constitutional reform reintroduced the post in April, and its holder would be expected to succeed Biya in the event of his death.

Questions about the president’s health have continued to swirl, with his frequent stays abroad fuelling debate over his ability to govern. Media debate about the president’s health, however, has been banned since 2024, when rumours circulated about his death.

In late August, Biya returned to Yaounde after more than two months in Geneva, drawing sharp criticism from the opposition.

Last month, the authorities suspended the Cameroon National Salvation Front (FSNC), the party of defeated opposition presidential candidate Issa Tchiroma Bakary.

Bakary went into exile in the Gambia after declaring himself the election winner and calling on supporters to defend his “victory”.
